- If sentiment shows strong bullish (e.g., +1.00) or bearish (-1.00) signals in recent days, model should adjust forecast directionally — avoid flat or trending forecasts when sentiment is polarized.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior day), model tends to overestimate continuation; reduce forecast slope or add early mean-reversion bias.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (e.g., 0.00 or 0.25), model often over-optimistically forecasts upward trend; cap forecast growth to 2–3% per day unless strong momentum signal.
- If true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., price drops after peak or rebounds after trough), model should reduce forecast momentum by 10–20% in subsequent days.
- For 30-day forecasts, model consistently overestimates near-term highs and underestimates lows — apply downward bias to later days if sentiment is weak or negative.
- If sentiment history includes multiple +1.00 or -1.00 entries, model should not ignore sentiment and adjust forecast range accordingly — avoid “neutral” forecasts when sentiment is volatile.
